slides.text: Gaind Singh became immortal as the first martyr in the history of Chhattisgarh. The soil of Dakshin Kosal lit up with the blood of its first martyr son, and this light further set fire to the piles of dry leaves of the rebellions.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Gaind Singh standing on a forest hilltop at dawn, traditional weapons in hand, British soldiers visible in the valley below. Dense Sal forest surrounds him. Ink-wash illustration, dark green and ochre, defiant and tragic mood.

slides.text: After ending the Halba rebellion of 1774, the Maratha ruler Diwans and the British completely engulfed the flags of their authority on the land of Bastar, and they started celebrating this victory by atrocities on the tribals of Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Maratha and British flags rising over the forts of Bastar, 1820s. Tribal villagers watching from the forest edge, fearful. Colonial occupation made visual — foreign flags on ancient soil. Dark sky, oppressive atmosphere, ink illustration.

slides.text: Unlimited harvesting of forest woods, taking work from the people here, excessive unnecessary taxes were collected on them. The interference of these tribes in their home — the forest — was not liked at all.
slides.visualDescription: British contractors cutting Sal trees in the tribal forest. Tribals watching helplessly as their forest is stripped. Stacks of lumber, colonial officers with ledgers collecting taxes. The forest — home, livelihood, identity — being destroyed.

slides.text: When the Bhonsle dynasty of Nagpur was defeated by the East India Company in 1818, the state of Chhattisgarh passed into the hands of the British based on the treaty. Then they started looting the public by establishing their state system here.
slides.visualDescription: Treaty signing scene — Bhonsle representatives and East India Company officers at a table. The map of Chhattisgarh changes hands. British administration machinery arriving — tax collectors, forest officers, revenue clerks. The occupation formalised.

slides.text: Seeing the ease of movement in the 1820s, the newly appointed Captain Pebe chose Paralkot as his stronghold. At that time the Raja was Mahipal Dev, who belonged to Ajmer Singh's lineage but was a supporter of the British.
slides.visualDescription: Captain Pebe on horseback surveying Paralkot — a forest-dwelling village on the banks of river Kotri where three rivers meet. A king in his palace who has chosen the British side. The stage being set for resistance. Colonial-era landscape.

slides.text: The Abhujmadi tribe was mainly in Paralkot. They could not tolerate the atrocities on them. Eventually in 1824, Gaind Singh, leading all the Abhujmadis, called for British-free Bastar — which became known as the Rebellion of Paralkot.
slides.visualDescription: Gaind Singh — the Zamindar of Paralkot — rising to address the Abhujmadi tribal assembly in the Ghotul. Firelight, forest, traditional weapons. A leader emerging. The declaration of resistance. Ink illustration, dramatic firelight.

slides.text: There were 165 villages within the Paralkot Zamindari, and Paralkot was the headquarters of the Zamindari. Paralkot, situated on the banks of river Kotri, is a forest-dwelling village near the Chandrapur district of Maharashtra, where three rivers meet.
slides.visualDescription: Map of Paralkot Zamindari — 165 villages marked, the river Kotri curving through dense forest. Three rivers meeting at Paralkot. The geography of the rebellion — forest as fortress, rivers as walls. Beautiful and strategic.

slides.text: The original purpose of the Rebellion of Paralkot was to free Bastar from outsiders. Abujhmad is made up of two words — Abujh, meaning 'that which cannot be understood,' and Maad, meaning 'mountain' in Gondi.
slides.visualDescription: The Abujhmad — mountains and dense forest, ancient and impenetrable. The meaning of the name written in Gondi script alongside its translation. A land that resists understanding, that hides its people. Sacred geography.

slides.text: The Ghotul is a spacious tribal hut surrounded by earthen or wooden walls. It is an integral part of Gond and Muria tribal life in regions of Chhattisgarh and the neighboring areas. Their meeting was held in Ghotul where the strategies of rebellion were made.
slides.visualDescription: Interior of a Ghotul at night — firelight, earthen walls, tribal elders and young warriors seated in a circle. Gaind Singh at the center, planning the rebellion. Bows, axes, and drums visible. A war council in sacred space.

slides.text: Angered by the presence of non-tribals in the tribal area and their arbitrariness, on January 4, 1825, after leaving the villages, caves, and mountain ranges, the tribals gathered at Paralkot. They were armed with their traditional weapons.
slides.visualDescription: January 1825. Abhujmadi warriors streaming from forest, caves, and mountain paths toward Paralkot. Men and women both, armed with bows, arrows, axes, spears. A gathering of defiance. Dawn light through Sal trees. Ink illustration.

slides.text: With the help of mountains and dense forests, the British were eluded for a year, which the British could not understand. The tribal forest became a strong weapon in front of the English guns.
slides.visualDescription: British soldiers lost in the dense Abujhmad forest — confused, unable to navigate. Tribal warriors watching from the treetops and behind rocks. The forest as ally, as weapon, as defender. Guerrilla warfare in ancient terrain.

slides.text: Abujhmadia used to come out in groups of five to five hundred. Some are led by women, some by men. And Gaind Singh kept leading them in a planned manner, using the guerilla method of war.
slides.visualDescription: Abhujmadi warriors emerging from the forest in disciplined groups — small teams and large formations. Women warriors leading some groups. Gaind Singh orchestrating the movement. Drums signaling. Guerrilla tactics in ancient forest.

slides.text: Thousands of forest dwellers started attacking by ambushing the English officers and Maratha employees with bows, arrows, and spears. Along with men, women were also participants in this rebellion — wherever the enemy could be seen, he would have been put to death.
slides.visualDescription: Ambush scene in the dense forest. Abhujmadi warriors rising from the undergrowth to attack a British patrol — bows drawn, spears raised. Men and women fighting side by side. Dynamic composition, action and courage. Ink illustration.

slides.text: They used to gather their comrades by playing the drums and attack the Marathas and British officers. The Abujhmadis have the distinction of fighting the British for the first time in the country — an armed resistance that began before 1857.
slides.visualDescription: Tribal drummer at the forest edge, drumbeat calling warriors from distant villages. The sound of the drum as a call to arms. In the distance, warriors emerging from the tree line. First resistance. First defiance. The beginning of a long war.

slides.text: British superintendent of Chhattisgarh, Agnew, had to intervene directly. Despite all the atrocities and lack of weapons, Abhujmadi Gaind Singh did not consider it appropriate to bow down.
slides.visualDescription: British Superintendent Agnew on horseback, dispatching orders. Gaind Singh in the forest, unbowed, continuing to lead. The contrast between colonial power and tribal dignity. One man with modern weapons. One man with arrows and resolve.

slides.text: Agnew called a large army from Chandrapur. The combined forces of the British and the Marathas laid siege to Paralkot on 10 January 1825 and surrounded Paralkot from all sides.
slides.visualDescription: The siege of Paralkot — British and Maratha forces encircling the forest village from all directions. January 10, 1825. Cannons, cavalry, modern weapons converging on a village of bows and spears. The encirclement tightening.

slides.text: The traditional weapons of the Abujhmadis failed to withstand the modern weaponry. Hundreds of Abujhmadis sacrificed their lives, but in front of the modern weapons of the British, the native guns and arrows of the Abujhmadis could not be effective.
slides.visualDescription: The final stand at Paralkot — arrows and spears against British rifles and cannons. Tribal warriors falling. The impossible courage of the outnumbered. Smoke and forest. The tragedy of asymmetric war. Somber ink illustration.

slides.text: Gaind Singh was arrested and with his arrest, the agitation came to a halt. The rebellion of Paralkot, which had kept the British at bay for months with forest, drums, and courage, was brought to an end.
slides.visualDescription: Gaind Singh in chains, surrounded by British soldiers. His head is still raised. The forest is quiet around him. Warriors watching from a distance, unable to help. The arrest of a leader — the silencing of a rebellion. Dignity in defeat.

slides.text: Ten days after his arrest, on January 20, 1825, Gaind Singh was hanged in front of the palace of Paralkot. Gaind Singh became immortal as the first martyr in the history of Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: January 20, 1825. The palace of Paralkot. Gaind Singh standing before the gallows, upright and unbroken. The Abhujmadi people watching. British soldiers with rifles. A moment of historical gravity. Dark sky, single shaft of light. Ink illustration.

slides.text: Gaind Singh, the Zamindar of Paralkot, has the title of Shaheed Shiromani — the crown of martyrs. While leading the first freedom struggle of Chhattisgarh, he laid down his life and sacrificed himself.
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of Gaind Singh — dignified, strong, looking into the distance. The title Shaheed Shiromani written beneath in Devanagari. Around him, the forest he loved, the rivers of Paralkot, the land he died for. Memorial portrait style.

slides.text: The soil of Dakshin Kosal — present-day Chhattisgarh — lit up with the blood of its first martyr son, and this light further set fire to the piles of dry leaves of the rebellions. A fire was lit that would not be extinguished.
slides.visualDescription: The soil of Chhattisgarh illuminated with a warm fire-like light. Dry leaves of the forest catching flame one by one across the map — each flame a future rebellion. Blood becoming light becoming fire. Visual metaphor of sacrifice and consequence.

slides.text: The Revolt of Halba 1774–79, led by Ajmer Singh, took place in the Dongar area against British armies and the Marathas. Raja Dalpat Singh of Bastar appointed his son Ajmer Singh as the governor of Dongar.
slides.visualDescription: Ajmer Singh of Dongar leading the Halba rebellion — warriors on horseback through forest. 1774. The Dongar area with its forts and forests. A chain of rebellion beginning before Paralkot. Timeline of resistance lit like a fuse.

slides.text: In the year 1774, when Dariyavdev became the new king of Bastar, he grossly neglected the Dongar area and started putting pressure on Ajmer Singh out of enmity. In the same year, there was a severe famine in the Dongar area and there was chaos.
slides.visualDescription: Famine in Dongar — parched fields, gaunt villagers, an indifferent king in his palace. Dariyavdev attacking Dongar while the famine rages. The double injustice of neglect and violence. Sepia tones, desperation and defiance.

slides.text: Daryavadev made separate treaties with the Company Government, the Marathas, and the Raja of Jaipur and prepared a large army of 20,000 soldiers. With the help of this army, he defeated the rebels at Jagdalpur. Ajmer Singh was killed in the battle.
slides.visualDescription: The battle at Jagdalpur — a 20,000-strong combined army against Halba rebels. The Halba rebels massacred on a large scale. Ajmer Singh falling in battle. The end of one rebellion — but the beginning of Bastar's subjugation to the Marathas and British.

slides.text: Thus, the Halba rebellion came to an end. But due to this, the position of the Raja of Jagdalpur became very weak. Bastar fell under the Maratha Bhonslas and paved the way for the arrival of the British in the future.
slides.visualDescription: The aftermath of the Halba rebellion — a weakened king, a land now under Maratha control, British interests watching from the distance. The path being cleared for colonial expansion. Seeds of future suffering sown in present defeat.

slides.text: The Revolt of Bhopalpatnam 1795 was limited and short-lived. When the British traveler Captain JT Blunt reached the border of Bastar, the tribals did not allow him, opposing his entry into Jagdalpur. Blunt was forced to return to Calcutta.
slides.visualDescription: Captain Blunt at the border of Bastar, 1795. Tribal warriors blocking the road with bows and spears. The Captain turning back. A small, brief, but proud moment of resistance. The forest as a gate that tribals controlled. Defiant stance.

slides.text: The Revolt of Tarapur 1842–54 saw Lal Dalganjan Singh, the governor of Tarapur, oppose increased taxation by the Maratha rule. The tribal farmers of Tarapur Pargana were facing many difficulties due to foreign rule — illegal taxes were being collected.
slides.visualDescription: Lal Dalganjan Singh — the governor of Tarapur — standing with farmers against a Maratha tax collector. The Pargana landscape of Tarapur. Another resistance, another brave leader. The pattern of tribal defiance continuing across decades.

slides.text: The Revolt of Meria 1842–63 was a rebellion against British interference in the local tradition of the Meria tribesmen at the Dantewada temple. Led by Hidma Manjhi, the Meria demanded the withdrawal of troops from the sacred site.
slides.visualDescription: The Dantewada temple — sacred, ancient. British soldiers deployed at its entrance to stop the practice of traditional sacrifice. Hidma Manjhi and the Meria tribesmen confronting them. A battle over faith and sovereignty.

slides.text: The Revolt of Koei 1859 saw local landlords and tribals of southern Bastar rise against British officers and outside contractors who were given the right to cut the forests. The rebels raised the slogan: 'Ek saal vriksh ke pichhe, ek vyakti ka sir.'
slides.visualDescription: Sal trees of Bastar — majestic, ancient. Contractors with axes backed by British gunmen. Tribal warriors with torches attacking the woodcutters. The slogan burning in the air: In revenge for a Sal tree, a person's head. Forest as identity.

slides.text: The Revolt of Muria 1876 saw the Muria tribesmen, led by Jhada Sirha, surround the palace on March 2, 1876. The rebels' one-point demand: Dewan Gopinath and Munshi Adil Prasad should be expelled from Bastar. Their demand was met — the Muria rebellion ended with success.
slides.visualDescription: Jhada Sirha leading Muria warriors to surround the king's palace. The palace fort encircled by tribal warriors with traditional weapons. Then: the Dewan expelled, the siege lifted, a rare moment of tribal victory. Success against the odds.

slides.text: The Revolt of Rani Choris 1878–82, also known as Rani Ka Kop — Queen's Wrath — saw Queen Jugraj Kunwar of Bastar revolt against the wrong actions of her husband Bhairamdev. British conspiracy was suspected behind this internal conflict.
slides.visualDescription: Queen Jugraj Kunwar of Bastar — regal, fierce, standing in her palace. The political division of Bastar into two factions. A woman's rebellion against her own king. The British shadow behind the conflict. Power, gender, and resistance.

slides.text: Each rebellion — Halba, Paralkot, Tarapur, Meria, Koei, Muria, Choris — forms a chain of fire across Chhattisgarh's history. Each martyr's blood watered the soil from which the next resistance grew.
slides.visualDescription: A timeline of flames — each rebellion a fire on the map of Chhattisgarh. From 1774 to 1882. Each flame feeding the next. A visual chain of sacrifice and defiance leading toward a greater conflagration. The genealogy of resistance.

slides.text: The area of Bastar division adjacent to the border of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh is called Paralkot. In this area now exists the city of Pakhanjur, and there are villages of Bengalis who have migrated from Bangladesh. The members of the Paralkot Zamindar family are leading a life of oblivion.
slides.visualDescription: Present-day Pakhanjur — a modern town where Paralkot once stood. Bengali migrant settlements. The descendants of Gaind Singh living in obscurity, their connection to history unrecognised. Memory erased, landscape changed. Melancholic.

slides.text: In the context of Chhattisgarh, the tribal movement means the movement of the tribals of Bastar, because Bastar is a tribal-dominated area and almost all the tribal movements have taken place in this region's Parganas.
slides.visualDescription: Map of Bastar showing all Parganas — each one a site of rebellion. The tribal geography of resistance. A land that defined its identity through its refusal to surrender. Ink-wash map, each rebellion site marked with a flame.

slides.text: Although the war of the land could not get respect in national history, it is still immortal in folk songs. The words recorded on the pages of history may be blurred, but the words inscribed in the mind, heart, and memory of the people are indelible.
slides.visualDescription: A tribal elder in present-day Bastar singing a folk song under a Sal tree, young children listening. The song carrying the names of the martyrs. Memory as music. History as living tradition. Warm afternoon light, continuity of resistance.

slides.text: Gaind Singh — Shaheed Shiromani — first martyr of Chhattisgarh. He died on January 20, 1825. He has no monument. He has no official remembrance. He has only this: the soil he bled for, and the fire he started that never went out.
slides.visualDescription: The banks of river Kotri at Paralkot — a simple, beautiful river landscape. No monument, no marker. Just water, forest, soil. The place where history happened and was forgotten. A candle flame reflected in the river. Memory over stone.

slides.text: But the fire never died. In 1910, the greatest tribal rebellion in Chhattisgarh's history would shake the earth of Bastar like an earthquake. Next: Episode 3 — The Earthquake of Bastar.
slides.visualDescription: The Sal forest of Bastar at night — quiet, immense, holding its secrets. Then: a tremor in the earth, leaves shaking, a drum beginning to beat in the distance. The buildup to something enormous. Title card: Episode 3 — The Earthquake of Bastar.
